title: Min Cost Climbing Stairs
statement: Each step of a staircase has a fee you pay when you leave it. You may start on step 0 or step 1, and each move climbs 1 or 2 steps. The top is one position past the last step. Find the smallest total fee to reach the top.

example.caption: Start on step 1 (free), pay 15 to jump two steps to the top. Total 15. Starting on step 0 and paying 10 then 20 costs 30.

output.label: dp[i] = cheapest way to stand on step i

idea.sentence: Let dp[i] be the cheapest total paid to stand on step i, then dp[i] = min(dp[i - 1] + cost[i - 1], dp[i - 2] + cost[i - 2]).

jargon.plain: What one table cell stands for. Here: the cheapest total paid to stand on step i, before paying that step's own fee.
The rule that builds a cell from earlier cells. Here: the cheaper of two ways in.

vars.meaning: number of steps (length of the cost list)

compare.unit: paths or cells (rough; paths grow like 1.6^n, which 2n stands in for)

rows.name: Plain recursion
rows.note: Every step branches into a 1-step and a 2-step and repeats work.

rows.name: DP table
rows.note: One cell per step, each from the two cells before it.

rows.name: Two variables
rows.note: Only the last two cells are ever read, so keep two numbers instead of the table.

fast.takeaway: Same shape as Climbing Stairs, but the cell holds a minimum cost instead of a count.

stages.title: Base cells
stages.note: dp has n + 1 cells. Starting on step 0 or step 1 is free, so both start at 0.

stages.title: Fill a cell
stages.note: Two ways in: from step i - 1 paying its fee, or from step i - 2 paying its fee. Keep the cheaper.

stages.title: Read the answer
stages.note: The top is index n, one past the last fee. dp[n] is the answer.

edges.title: Two steps only
edges.why: Start on step 1 and jump straight to the top paying 3. The table has 3 cells, so dp[2] = min(0 + 5, 0 + 3).

edges.title: Starting step matters
edges.why: Starting on step 1 skips the first 100. Both start cells are 0 because both starts are free.

edges.title: Huge first fee
edges.why: You never have to pay cost[0] if you start on step 1.

edges.title: Zero fees
edges.why: Leave step 1 by a 2-step to land on step 3, then another to the top. The 50 is jumped over.

gotchas.text: The top is index n, not n - 1. Returning dp[n - 1] is the usual off-by-one, and reaching the last step is not yet reaching the top.
The fee is paid when you leave a step, so dp[i] adds cost[i - 1] and cost[i - 2], not cost[i].
Math.min(...) is fine for two numbers. Do not spread a big array into it, because very long argument lists can overflow the call stack.
The built-in min needs Go 1.21 or newer. On older versions, write a small helper.

recap.pattern: 1-D DP: cheaper of two ways in
recap.key: dp[i] = cheapest total to stand on step i = min(dp[i - 1] + cost[i - 1], dp[i - 2] + cost[i - 2]). The answer is dp[n].
recap.complexity: Time O(n). Space O(n), or O(1) with two variables.
moves: Cell meaning: dp[i] = cheapest cost to stand on step i
